summary:
The British Virgin Islands is a British Overseas Territory. Its sodomy laws were repealed by order of the United Kingdom's Privy Council in January 2001, one of five remaining British Caribbean territories in which the United Kingdom's highest court of appeal acted after the local legislatures refused to do so. Local legislator Orlando Smith conceded the position publicly at the time, saying "there is nothing we can do." The repeal came from outside the territory's own institutions rather than from the House of Assembly, and United Kingdom legislation reaches the islands through Orders in Council rather than by automatic extension.

Local law does not provide for marriage between two people of the same sex. Whether a marriage contracted in the United Kingdom between Kinisha Forbes and Kirsten Lettsome is valid in the territory was litigated before Justice Adrian Jack, and in July 2022 the BVI Christian Council lost its bid to appeal his case-management orders. The substantive question of local recognition was not resolved in the reporting available.

A trans visitor faces no criminal exposure for same-sex intimacy. Partner recognition is unsettled rather than settled in either direction: a marriage contracted abroad between two women is contested, and a trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under local law has no recognition to rely on.
tangentialFactors:
The 2001 repeal covered four other British Caribbean territories alongside the British Virgin Islands, so decriminalisation here followed a regional pattern imposed through the same court of appeal rather than a local political decision.

A source published in 2012 and updated in 2017 describes same-sex life in the territory as lived discreetly, with hostility it characterises as silent and invisible rather than openly expressed. That assessment predates the 2022 marriage litigation and is a source characterisation rather than a documented enforcement record.
localsOnly: Residents have no local legislative route to marriage recognition. The House of Assembly declined to act on the criminal-law question in 2001, and the litigation over the Forbes and Lettsome marriage has run through the courts rather than the legislature. The BVI Christian Council's intervention in that case shows organised local opposition to recognition.
outOfScopeNotes:
The substantive ruling on whether the Forbes and Lettsome marriage is valid under British Virgin Islands law is not established by the sources available; only the procedural appeal outcome of July 2022 is documented.

No trans-specific law, policy, enforcement action, document or marker rule, healthcare provision, or facilities rule for the territory appears in the source inventory.
